title: Cognitive Set 06: Alternating Work, Escalators & Reasoning
description: Tests alternate-day work, moving walkways, chord geometry, stars-and-bars combinatorics, error-rate DI, and verbal logic.

questions.question: A can design a database schema in 12 days and B can do the same job in 18 days. If they work on alternate days starting with A on Day 1, in how many days will the work be completed?
questions.explanation: Total work = LCM(12, 18) = 36 units. A = 3 units/day, B = 2 units/day. One 2-day cycle (A then B) completes 3 + 2 = 5 units. Seven full cycles (14 days) complete 7 * 5 = 35 units. Remaining 1 unit is done by A on Day 15 in 1/3 day. Total time = 14 1/3 days.
questions.shortcut: Cycle(2d) = 5/36 => 7 cycles = 14d (35 units); 1 unit by A at 3/d = 1/3 day => 14 1/3.

questions.question: A commuter walks up a rising escalator in 40 seconds. Walking at the exact same speed down the same rising escalator (against its motion), he takes 120 seconds. How many seconds would it take if he stood still on the rising escalator?
questions.explanation: Let escalator length = N, person speed = p, escalator speed = e. Going with escalator: N / (p + e) = 40; against escalator: N / (p - e) = 120. Dividing gives (p + e)/(p - e) = 3 => p + e = 3p - 3e => 2p = 4e => p = 2e. Then N = 40 * (2e + e) = 120e. Standing still, time = N / e = 120 seconds.
questions.shortcut: Time standing = 2 * t1 * t2 / (t2 - t1) = (2 * 40 * 120) / 80 = 120 seconds.

questions.question: X and Y invest Rs. 50,000 and Rs. 70,000 respectively in a consultancy. X receives 10% of the total profit as a management allowance, and the remaining profit is divided in proportion to their capitals. If total annual profit is Rs. 60,000, what is X's total share?
questions.explanation: X's management allowance = 10% of 60,000 = Rs. 6,000. Remaining profit = 60,000 - 6,000 = Rs. 54,000, shared in ratio 5 : 7. X's capital share = (5 / 12) * 54,000 = Rs. 22,500. Total for X = 6,000 + 22,500 = Rs. 28,500.

questions.question: What is the smallest 4-digit integer that leaves a remainder of 7 when divided by each of 12, 15, and 18?
questions.explanation: LCM(12, 15, 18) = 180. Any such number has form 180k + 7. For k = 5, 907 (3 digits). For k = 6, 180*6 + 7 = 1,087 (smallest 4-digit match).
questions.shortcut: LCM(12,15,18) = 180; smallest 4-digit multiple is 1080; add 7 => 1087.

questions.question: A 20% reduction in the price of RAM modules enables a university lab to buy 5 more modules for Rs. 4,000. What was the original price of one RAM module?
questions.explanation: A 20% savings on Rs. 4,000 is Rs. 800, which buys the 5 extra modules at the REDUCED price. Thus reduced price = 800 / 5 = Rs. 160. Since 160 = 80% of original price, original price = 160 / 0.8 = Rs. 200.
questions.shortcut: 20% of 4000 = 800 buys 5 extra => new price = 160 => old price = 160/0.8 = 200.

questions.question: A tray contains 15 microcontrollers, of which 3 are defective. Two microcontrollers are picked at random without replacement. What is the probability that at least one of them is defective?
questions.explanation: Complement P(both non-defective) = C(12, 2) / C(15, 2) = 66 / 105 = 22 / 35. Therefore P(at least one defective) = 1 - 22/35 = 13/35.

questions.question: Two parallel chords of lengths 16 cm and 12 cm lie on opposite sides of the center of a circle of radius 10 cm. What is the perpendicular distance between the two chords?
questions.explanation: Perpendicular from center bisects each chord. Distance of 16 cm chord from center = sqrt(10^2 - 8^2) = 6 cm. Distance of 12 cm chord from center = sqrt(10^2 - 6^2) = 8 cm. On opposite sides, distance between chords = 6 + 8 = 14 cm.
questions.shortcut: Pythagorean triples (6,8,10): distances are 6 and 8; opposite sides => 6 + 8 = 14 cm.

questions.question: How many non-negative integer solutions (x, y, z) satisfy the equation x + y + z = 12?
questions.explanation: By the stars-and-bars theorem, the number of non-negative integer solutions to x1 + x2 + ... + xk = n is C(n + k - 1, k - 1). Here C(12 + 3 - 1, 3 - 1) = C(14, 2) = (14 * 13) / 2 = 91.

Seven server blades B1 through B7 are stacked vertically in slots 1 (bottom) to 7 (top). B3 is in slot 4. Exactly two blades sit between B3 and B6. B1 sits immediately above B6. B5 sits immediately below B3. B2 sits immediately above B4, and B7 sits somewhere above B2. Which blade sits in slot 5?
questions.explanation: B3 = 4 and B5 = 3 (immediately below B3). Two slots between B3(4) and B6 allow B6 = 1 or 7; since B1 is immediately above B6, B6 = 1 and B1 = 2. Remaining slots {5, 6, 7} hold B4, B2, and B7. Because B2 is immediately above B4 and B7 is above B2, the order must be B4=5, B2=6, B7=7. Thus B4 sits in slot 5.
questions.shortcut: Bottom-to-top 1..7: B6, B1, B5, B3, B4, B2, B7 => slot 5 is B4.

questions.question: Statements: (1) All REST APIs are stateless. (2) Some stateless services are GraphQL endpoints. (3) No GraphQL endpoint uses SOAP. Conclusions: I. Some stateless services do not use SOAP. II. No REST API uses SOAP.
questions.explanation: Stateless services overlapping GraphQL endpoints cannot use SOAP, proving Conclusion I. However, REST APIs and GraphQL endpoints have no required overlap or exclusion with SOAP outside GraphQL, so II is not guaranteed.
questions.shortcut: Stateless ∩ GraphQL != empty and GraphQL ∩ SOAP = empty => I holds; no direct link for REST vs SOAP.

questions.question: Given: X $ Y means X is the husband of Y; X @ Y means X is the daughter of Y; X # Y means X is the brother of Y. In the expression 'K @ M # N $ P', how is K related to N?
questions.explanation: K @ M means K is the daughter of M. M # N means M is the brother of N (and N $ P confirms N is the husband of P). Since K is the daughter of N's brother M, K is N's niece.
questions.shortcut: K is daughter of M, and M is brother of N => K is N's niece.

What is Priya's present age? Statement I: Five years ago, Priya was three times as old as her cousin Tara. Statement II: Five years from now, Priya will be twice as old as Tara.
options: Both statements I and II together are necessary
questions.explanation: I gives P - 5 = 3(T - 5) => P - 3T = -10 (two unknowns). II gives P + 5 = 2(T + 5) => P - 2T = 5 (two unknowns). Subtracting yields T = 15 and P = 35 uniquely. Both are necessary.
questions.shortcut: Two independent linear equations in two variables (P, T) => need both.

questions.question: A campus shuttle leaves the North Gate heading South for 4 km, turns left and drives 3 km, turns left and drives 4 km, then turns right and drives 5 km. How far and in which direction is it from the North Gate?
questions.explanation: Start (0,0): South 4 => (0,-4); left (East) 3 => (3,-4); left (North) 4 => (3,0); right (East) 5 => (8,0). It is 8 km due East of the North Gate.
questions.shortcut: North-South cancels (-4 + 4 = 0); Eastward segments = 3 + 5 = 8 km East.

questions.question: In a single-file queue, Ravi is 14th from the front and Meena is 19th from the rear. If there are exactly 6 people standing between Ravi and Meena, what is the MINIMUM possible total number of people in the queue?
questions.explanation: For minimum queue length, Ravi and Meena must overlap (Meena is ahead of Ravi). Minimum total = (Front rank + Rear rank) - Between - 2 = (14 + 19) - 6 - 2 = 33 - 8 = 25 (verify: Meena at pos 7 from front, Ravi at pos 14 from front => 6 people at pos 8..13 between them, and Meena is 19th from rear => total = 7 + 19 - 1 = 25).
questions.shortcut: Overlap minimum = L + R - B - 2 = 14 + 19 - 6 - 2 = 25.

questions.question: Question: Should technical campus interviews eliminate live whiteboard coding and rely solely on take-home projects? Argument I: Yes, take-home projects mirror real engineering workflows with IDE tooling and documentation. Argument II: No, without a live verification round, hiring teams cannot confirm the candidate actually wrote and understands the submitted solution.
options: Both Arguments I and II are strong
Neither Argument I nor II is strong
questions.explanation: Argument I presents a practical validity point (realism of IDE workflows). Argument II presents an equally compelling integrity point (verifying authorship and comprehension). Both are substantive and strong.
questions.shortcut: Both address real, distinct engineering hiring trade-offs (realism vs authorship verification).

questions.question: Which upcoming calendar year after 2026 will have the EXACT same day-of-week calendar as the year 2026?
questions.explanation: Count odd days starting from 2026 (ordinary year): 2026(+1), 2027(+1), 2028(+2, leap), 2029(+1), 2030(+1), 2031(+1) -> sum = 7 (0 mod 7), wait: 2032 is a leap year so 2032 only matches Jan-Feb of 2026! Keep counting: 2032(+2)->9, 2033(+1)->10, 2034(+1)->11, 2035(+1)->12, 2036(+2)->14 (0 mod 7)! And 2037 is an ordinary year! Thus 2037 matches 2026 completely (+11 rule for year = leap+2).
questions.shortcut: 2026 is (leap + 2): ordinary year (leap+2) repeats after +11 years => 2026 + 11 = 2037.

questions.passage: Observability platforms generate immense telemetry volumes—traces, structured logs, and high-cardinality metrics—that can easily cost more to store than the production servers being monitored. Simply sampling one percent of traces uniformly reduces storage bills, yet risks discarding the very five-hundred-millisecond outliers and 5xx failures engineers need during an incident. Tail-based sampling resolves this tension by buffering spans briefly at the collector tier and retaining 100 percent of erroneous or slow traces while aggressively downsampling routine healthy traffic.
questions.question: Why does uniform random sampling of traces fall short during production incidents?
options: Collectors lack sufficient RAM to buffer healthy requests
Uniform sampling often drops rare slow outliers and 5xx error traces needed for debugging
High-cardinality metrics cannot be stored alongside structured logs
Uniform sampling increases storage costs beyond production server bills
questions.explanation: The passage notes that uniform 1% sampling 'risks discarding the very five-hundred-millisecond outliers and 5xx failures engineers need during an incident.'
questions.shortcut: Look directly at sentence 2 ('risks discarding...').

questions.passage: Observability platforms generate immense telemetry volumes—traces, structured logs, and high-cardinality metrics—that can easily cost more to store than the production servers being monitored. Simply sampling one percent of traces uniformly reduces storage bills, yet risks discarding the very five-hundred-millisecond outliers and 5xx failures engineers need during an incident. Tail-based sampling resolves this tension by buffering spans briefly at the collector tier and retaining 100 percent of erroneous or slow traces while aggressively downsampling routine healthy traffic.
questions.question: How does tail-based sampling balance observability cost against diagnostic fidelity?
options: It deletes all traces once a microservice returns HTTP 200
It buffers spans briefly to keep all slow or failing traces while heavily sampling routine ones
It shifts telemetry storage directly onto end-user browsers
It disables structured logging on production servers
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 states that tail-based sampling buffers spans briefly at the collector tier to keep 100% of erroneous/slow traces while downsampling healthy traffic.
questions.shortcut: Match sentence 3 word-for-word on buffering spans + keeping 100% of error/slow traces.

questions.question: Identify the grammatical error: 'The security team succeeded to block (A) / the credential-stuffing attack (B) / within three minutes of (C) / receiving the anomaly alert. (D)'
questions.explanation: The verb 'succeed' takes the preposition 'in' followed by a gerund ('succeeded in blocking'), not an infinitive ('succeeded to block').
questions.shortcut: Idiom: 'succeed in + V-ing' (not 'succeed to + V1').

questions.question:
Arrange P, Q, R, S coherently:
P. Without clear rollback scripts, however, a backward-incompatible column drop can trap teams in hours of downtime.
Q. Continuous delivery encourages shipping small database migrations alongside application code.
R. Separating destructive drops into a delayed cleanup release after all old app pods terminate avoids this trap.
S. When a new schema adds an optional column, existing application instances continue operating smoothly.
questions.explanation: Q introduces database migrations in CD. S illustrates the safe additive case ('optional column'). P introduces the contrasting destructive risk ('column drop... trap teams'). R explains how to avoid 'this trap'. Order: Q-S-P-R.
questions.shortcut: Safe case (S) -> Risk 'trap' (P) -> Avoiding 'this trap' (R).

questions.question: Select the correct improvement: 'Since the team adopted automated static analysis, production null-pointer incidents [dropped] by seventy percent.'
questions.explanation: When 'since + simple past' marks a starting point leading up to the present, the main clause requires the present perfect tense ('have dropped').
questions.shortcut: 'Since + past event' => main clause uses present perfect ('have dropped').

questions.question: Fill in the blanks: 'Rather than issuing ______ apologies after every outage, the vendor published a ______ engineering roadmap with measurable SLO targets.'
questions.explanation: 'Perfunctory' (routine/hollow) contrasts sharply with 'concrete' (specific, backed by measurable SLO targets).
questions.shortcut: 'Rather than' sets up hollow ('perfunctory') vs actionable ('concrete').

questions.question: Spot the error: 'Although the new query optimizer runs fastly (A) / on small test fixtures, (B) / it degrades sharply (C) / on multi-million-row joins. (D)'
questions.explanation: 'Fast' is both an adjective and an adverb; 'fastly' is not a standard English word. Segment (A) should read 'runs fast'.
questions.shortcut: Never use 'fastly'; the adverb form of 'fast' is 'fast'.

questions.question:
Order P, Q, R, S logically:
P. Once a consensus quorum acknowledges the append, the leader advances its commit index and replies to the client.
Q. In Raft-based distributed stores, all client writes flow through an elected leader node.
R. If the leader crashes mid-round, any follower holding the most up-to-date log is eligible to win the next election.
S. The leader appends the command to its local write-ahead log and replicates entries in parallel to follower nodes.
questions.explanation: Q introduces the leader role. S describes appending & replicating to followers. P describes quorum acknowledgment & client reply ('Once a consensus quorum acknowledges...'). R covers failover if the leader crashes. Order: Q-S-P-R.
questions.shortcut: Leader receives write (Q) -> Replicates (S) -> Quorum commits (P) -> Crash recovery (R).

questions.question: Choose the clearest correction: 'Each of the backend services [have their own] dedicated PostgreSQL schema.'
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular and takes a singular verb ('has') and singular pronoun ('its').
questions.shortcut: 'Each of the [plural]' always takes singular verb + singular pronoun ('has its own').

questions.question: Observation: 'After Company Z replaced rigid 9-to-5 office attendance with asynchronous remote work, average daily Slack messages fell by 35%, yet on-time sprint delivery rose by 18%.' Which option best explains both outcomes?
options: Developers stopped collaborating on complex architectural tickets altogether
Replacing fragmented real-time chat interruptions with structured written design docs freed deep-focus coding blocks
Company Z hired fewer QA testers during the transition quarter
Slack experienced two brief regional outages during the quarter
questions.explanation: Moving from noisy real-time chat to structured async documentation naturally drops message counts while giving engineers uninterrupted focus blocks that improve sprint delivery.
questions.shortcut: Need one cause explaining BOTH fewer chat messages AND higher sprint delivery.
